unit_label: CB Module C unit 3: fiscal-monetary relations (courseware unit 9)

facts.statement: Monetary-fiscal relations in India (courseware): harmonisation of monetary and fiscal policies is a prerequisite for attaining the twin objectives of growth and stability. The major objective of central banks is to ensure price stability with growth; Robert Barro suggested that high inflation levels are inimical to growth and optimal growth is possible only when inflation is below 7 per cent. A major contributing factor for monetary expansion has been the fiscal policies adopted over the years; since 1951, Government faced huge fiscal deficits; the financing of these deficits was met by the RBI through what are called ad hoc Treasury Bills; the maturity of Treasury Bills is 3 months; if the Government fails to meet its obligations in 3 months, it had to renew such bills for longer periods; over time this practice had become automatic and such financing of Government expenditure was known as automatic monetisation. The RBI played a crucial role in bridging the resource gap of the Government in plan financing by monetising government debt and maintaining interest rates at artificially low levels for government securities to reduce the cost of government borrowing; this policy is also known as accommodative monetary policy in the sense that the RBI accommodates the Government towards meeting its financing needs; inevitably such a policy had led to inflationary pressures in the economy and led to financial repression; also this accommodative monetary policy weakened RBI primary objective of maintaining price stability; the growth rate in the Indian economy remained quite low (around 3 per cent) up to the 1980s and moved to around 5 per cent in 1985. Striking balance between inflation and growth: the twin objectives of growth with price stability cannot be met unless there is better harmonisation of monetary and fiscal policies; the ushering in of the financial sector reforms and the Several initiatives have been taken in recent years to impart greater autonomy and independence to the central bank; the major steps in this direction have been (a) putting an end to automatic monetisation, and (b) stipulating a ceiling on public debt by passing the FRBM (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management) Act; the most striking feature has been the greater co-ordination achieved between the fiscal and monetary authorities over the years on matters of fiscal-monetary relevance. The monetary policy formulation assumes paramount importance in containing inflation in terms of ensuring that (a) monetary expansion is in line with the productive capacity of the country, (b) credit flows into the most productive sectors of the economy and not diverted in to speculative or unproductive activities. The Reserve Bank of India has adopted the best global standards and practices in the conduct of monetary policy and has moved beyond the frontiers of monetary management to embrace the wider mandate of financial stability. A major challenge in striking a balance between inflation and growth stems from excessive capital inflows; central banks need to immobilise these flows in case the country is unable to absorb these flows through investments in the most productive channels; the Reserve Bank of India in co-ordination with the Government of India has introduced the Market Stabilisation Scheme in terms of sterilisation of the excessive flows that are immobilised through the issue of Market Stabilisation Bonds (MSBs) so as to curb the inflationary pressures in the economy. Against the backdrop of GDP growth moving to around 8-10 per cent in the past even when other countries were seeing declines in their growth rates, inflation has been high during 2009-10 and 2010-11 and Reserve Bank of India has been focusing on the issue and trying to control the same; the Reserve Bank has been consistently trying to rein in inflation using the then available policy instrument, the repo rate, which was changed more than 10 times in the previous two years (2009-11); the Central Bank is trying to anchor inflationary expectations while at the same time trying to maintain growth momentum. Subir Gokarn studied the issue of growth-inflation trade off and provided evidence to the contrary: his graph relating decadal averages of growth and inflation shows that there has been a steady upward movement in the growth rate accompanied by a steady downward movement in the inflation rate over the last several decades; the contrast is even more striking when the agricultural sector, the slowest growing among the three, is removed from the growth calculations; the evidence suggests that there is no long-term trade-off between growth and inflation; if anything, accelerating growth is accompanied by decelerating inflation.

Recent finances of the Centre and States (courseware): an important factor that heightens the prospects of the recovery is the fiscal policy stance; the thrust on infrastructure can create conditions for broadening the revival in economic activity by exploiting forward and backward linkages and multiplier effects. The Union Budget 2021-22 announcement for setting up a Development Financial Institution (DFI) with a capital base of Rs 20,000 crore to finance projects under the National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP) aims to address the problem of long-term project financing. Recognising the risks to the recovery from a premature fiscal tightening, the central government has opted for a gradual fiscal consolidation by budgeting the gross fiscal deficit (GFD) at 6.8 per cent of GDP in 2021-22 (down from 9.4 per cent in the preceding year) and bringing it down gradually to below 4.5 per cent of GDP by 2025-26; the Government budgeted a higher capital outlay; states have budgeted a consolidation in the GFD at around 3.2 per cent of GSDP in 2021-22 (based on budgets of 17 states) keeping in view the Fifteenth Finance Commission target of 4.0 per cent. Given the adverse impact of COVID-19 on state finances, the Reserve Bank increased ways and means advances (WMA) limit in April 2020 by 60 per cent over and above the level as on March 31, 2020; this was extended for a further period of 6 months till March 31, 2021, and then, based on the recommendations of the Advisory Committee on WMA to State Governments (2021) (Chairman: Shri Sudhir Shrivastava), the existing interim limit was extended for further six months, up to September 30, 2021; the number of days for overdraft (OD) was increased till March 31, 2021 and then extended till September 2021 in May 2021; the Reserve Bank relaxed the rules governing withdrawal from the consolidated sinking fund (CSF) to enable states to meet a larger proportion of their market borrowings redemption; the Centre has allocated Rs 15,000 crore under the scheme of Special Assistance to States for Capital Expenditure for 2021-22 as interest-free 50-year loans, which is in addition to Rs 11,830 crore released to states in 2020-21 as part of the Aatma Nirbhar Bharat package to carry out capital expenditure; based on the 15th Finance Commission recommendation, the Centre has allowed states a net market borrowing of up to 4 per cent of GSDP for the year 2021-22, with a flexibility to go beyond 4 per cent on fulfilment of power sector reforms. Central government finances in 2020-21: in the wake of the pandemic, the Union Government announced a series of economic reform measures which cumulatively amounted to Rs 17.2 lakh crore (9.3 per cent of GDP); the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Package (PMGKP, 26 March 2020) focused on protecting lives and livelihoods of vulnerable sections; Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan 1.0 (May 13-17) focused on providing liquidity support through government guarantees and low interest rate loans to micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), microfinance institutions (MFIs), housing finance companies (HFCs) and power distribution companies (DISCOMs); Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan 2.0 (October 12) included consumption-based measures such as leave travel concession (LTC) cash voucher scheme and interest free loans for government employees and investment in the form of increase in the capital expenditure budget of the Union Government; Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan 3.0 (November 12) included additional outlay for Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana - Urban, further increase in the capex budget, equity infusion in the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) and a production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme for 10 identified sectors to boost domestic manufacturing, investment and employment. The total fiscal package does not reflect the true fiscal cost to the Union Government as it includes below the line items like liquidity support measures as well; the total expenditure of the Union Government increased from Rs 30.4 lakh crore in BE to Rs 34.5 lakh crore in RE, also including the increase in expenditure arising on account of off-budgeting of a large part of outstanding food bills availed in lieu of subsidies by the Food Corporation of India (FCI) from the National Small Savings Fund (NSSF). Central finances in 2021-22: the Union Budget 2021-22 set the stage for a strong revival by increasing the buoyancy of tax revenue through improved compliance, and by increased receipts from monetisation of assets; the Budget aims at improving tax buoyancy and better compliance through data analytics and artificial intelligence; the scope of faceless assessment has been broadened; a renewed push to disinvestment and asset monetisation in the budget through the new public sector enterprise policy, which aims to minimise the presence of central public sector enterprises (CPSEs) and create more space for the private sector; four broad strategic areas (atomic energy, space and defence; power, petroleum, coal and minerals; transport and telecommunications; and financial services) have been identified where CPSEs will have a minimal presence; in the counter-cyclical fiscal support to the economy is to be maintained through capital expenditure, which is expected to increase to 2.5 per cent of GDP from an average of 1.7 per cent during 2010-20; the sizeable deviation in gross fiscal deficit in 2020-21 and 2021-22 has necessitated a quantum jump in market borrowings of the Union Government, which remain the primary source of financing the deficit, followed by access to the NSSF. State finances: the provisional accounts for states for H1:2020-21 indicate that the GFD-GSDP ratio stood at 3.8 per cent against the budget estimate of 2.8 per cent for the year; the revenue receipts of state governments recovered partially with gradual resumption in economic activity; states revenue expenditure remained muted initially; typically states have a tendency to cut back their capital expenditure by on average 0.5 per cent of GDP; as per information for 17 state governments, the GFD has been budgeted at 3.2 per cent of GSDP in 2021-22 as against 4.1 per cent in 2020-21 (RE); this is in line with the Fifteenth Finance Commission (FC-XV) recommendation on the revised fiscal roadmap for states; the consolidation over the previous year has been sought to be achieved primarily through enhanced revenue receipts and cut in revenue expenditure while hiking capex; states, which have been under stress on the revenue front, are likely to get some support from FC-XV recommendations, particularly with respect to grants, which are slated to rise in the award period.

Finance Commission (courseware): the Constitution of India provides for the establishment of a Finance Commission for the purpose of allocation of certain resources of revenue between the Union and the State Governments; a Finance Commission is established under Article 280 of the Constitution of India by the President of India for the purpose of devolution of financial resources from the central government to state governments; the qualifications, powers, and procedures of the Commission itself are regulated by the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1951; such commissions are deemed to be civil courts for the purposes of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898; these commissions are appointed for a period of 5 years. Functions: under Article 280 of the Constitution the Finance Commission is required to make recommendations to the President in respect of: (1) the distribution between the Union and the States of the net proceeds of taxes to be shared between them, and the allocation between the States, the respective share of such proceeds; (2) the principles which should govern the grants-in-aid by the Centre to States out of the Consolidated Fund of India; (3) the measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of the Panchayats and the Municipalities in the state on the basis of the recommendations made by the State Finance Commission; (4) any other matter referred to it by the President in the interests of sound finance. The first Finance Commission (FC-1) was appointed by the President of India in 1951 under the Chairmanship of Mr K.C. Neogy; these Commissions played a major role in developing the principles and practice of transferring resources from centre to states, keeping in view the imperatives of the planning process and the need to bring the undeveloped/underdeveloped states on the growth path; to achieve the set objectives, the Finance Commission developed various criteria such as demographic condition, per capita income, income distance, forest cover etc. for ensuring equity in the distribution of resources among states. The Fifteenth Finance Commission (FC-15) was constituted by the President under Article 280 of the Constitution on 27 November 2017 to make recommendations for the period 2021-26; Shri N.K. Singh, former Member of Parliament and former Secretary to the Government of India was appointed as the Chairman of the Commission; the full report of the FC-15 covering the period 2021-26 was submitted on November 9, 2020 and was placed before the Parliament on February 1, 2021. Table 9.5 lists the Finance Commissions appointed so far (FC1 in 1951, chair K.C. Neogy, 1952-57; FC15 in 2017, chair N.K. Singh, 2017-22 as the operational duration in the table); other chairmen include K. Santhanam (FC2), A.K. Chanda (FC3), P.V. Rajamannar (FC4), Mahaveer Tyagi (FC5), K. Brahmananda Reddy (FC6), J.M. Shelat (FC7), Y.B. Chavan (FC8), N.K.P. Salve (FC9), K.C. Pant (FC10), A.M. Khusro (FC11), C. Rangarajan (FC12), Vijay Kelkar (FC13), Dr Y.V. Reddy (FC14).

Recommendations of the Fifteenth Finance Commission (courseware): there are three aspects of the recommendations in a historical context: tax devolution, grants, and fiscal roadmap/rules. Tax devolution: the base of union taxes shareable with the states was considerably widened by the Eleventh Finance Commission (FC-11) which recommended that all union taxes, excluding cesses and surcharges, should be shareable with states (earlier only excise duty and income tax collections were shareable); since then, successive finance commissions have made increments in the devolution ratio, with the Fourteenth Finance Commission (FC-14) making a radical departure by recommending a significantly higher share in view of the abolition of the planning commission and cessation of plan grants, thus making tax devolution the primary vehicle for federal transfers. Nevertheless, the increase in devolution ratio did not translate into a commensurate rise in the devolved taxes due to the proliferation of cesses and surcharges that are excluded from the divisible pool of union taxes; FC-15 was guided by stability and continuity in tax transfers and has maintained the tax devolution ratio (adjusting for the share attributable to Jammu and Kashmir) recommended by its predecessor. As regards the inter se distribution of taxes among states (horizontal sharing), equity-based criteria have dominated in determining the share of individual states since the Eighth Finance Commission (FC-8), thus making the tax devolution progressive. In case of the FC-15, the most significant change in the criteria for determining the share of individual states is to move the population census from 1971 to 2011; it has introduced a new criterion of demographic performance, the product of the inverse of the total fertility rate as per 2011 population census, and a state population in 1971, to reward states that have successfully brought down population growth. The other major change is the re-introduction of the criterion for tax effort that was used by the 10th, 11th and 12th Finance Commissions, but was done away with by the 13th and 14th Finance Commissions. Grants-in-aid: the FC-XV has made a significant departure from its predecessor in recommending a historically high share of grants in total transfers; compositionally, grants to local bodies have the highest share in finance commission grants since the FC-XIII, followed by post devolution revenue deficit grants, both of which have seen their share in total transfers rise consecutively in the last two finance commission recommendations; the FC-XV has brought back sector- and state-specific grants that were a regular feature till the FC-XIII; the Union Government has, however, indicated that it will give due consideration to these grants while revisiting the centrally sponsored schemes. Fiscal roadmap/rules: successive finance commissions have recommended debt and deficit targets as well as institutional changes to make governments accountable and transparent in the conduct of fiscal policy; the FC-12, the FC-13 and the FC-14 recommended elimination of revenue deficits and limiting the fiscal deficit to GDP ratio to 3 per cent under both levels of governments; as regards institutional measures, FC-12 recommended the creation of a sinking fund for debt repayments and a guarantee redemption fund to safeguard states finances from invocation of guarantees, both of which have been implemented by majority of states; the FC-XIV recommended exclusion of state governments from NSSF operations from April 1, 2015 (existing obligations on servicing and repayment to be fulfilled). The FC-15 has made significant relaxations in the fiscal deficit and debt targets in view of the pandemic induced slowdown; the gross fiscal deficit (GFD) for the Union Government is recommended on an elevated path with the terminal year (2025-26) target in the range of 3.5 to 4.5 per cent of GDP and the combined net borrowing limit of state governments has been relaxed to 4 per cent of GSDP in 2021-22 and 3.5 per cent of GSDP in 2022-23, with an additional allowance of 0.5 per cent for the four year period of 2021-22 to 2024-25 conditioned upon improvement in operational and financial performance of power distribution companies (DISCOMs). The targets are set for the government as per the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 to establish fiscal discipline in the economy, reduce fiscal deficit and improve the management of public funds; the FRBM Act also sets target for the government to bring down fiscal deficit. Fiscal road map recommended by the 15th Finance Commission: GFD-GDP ratio glide path from 9.3 per cent in 2021-22 to 6.8 per cent in 2025-26; projected debt/GDP ratio of 85.7 per cent in 2025-26 after peaking at 89.6 per cent in 2022-23; restructuring of FRBM and timetable for achieving debt sustainability to be examined by a high powered inter-departmental group; for states, in the baseline scenario the GFD-GSDP ratio glide path from 6 per cent in 2021-22 to 4 per cent in 2025-26; projected debt-GDP ratio of 56.6 per cent in 2025-26 after peaking at 62.9 per cent in 2021-22; normal limit of net borrowings to be 4 per cent in 2021-22, 3.5 per cent in 2022-23 and 3 per cent of GSDP from 2023-24 to 2025-26; incentive based additional borrowings of 0.5 per cent of GSDP from 2021-22 to 2024-25.

payload.title: Monetary-fiscal relations in India: automatic monetisation and the inflation-growth balance
payload.core_explanation_md:
**The link:** **harmonising monetary and fiscal policy** is a **prerequisite** for **growth with stability**. **Barro**: **optimal growth** needs inflation **below about 7 per cent**.

**History:** since **1951** the Government ran **large deficits** that the **RBI financed through ad hoc Treasury Bills** (**3-month** bills **renewed** each time, so financing became **automatic**): **automatic monetisation**. The RBI also **bridged the plan resource gap** by **monetising debt** and keeping **government security yields artificially low**: an **accommodative** policy that caused **inflationary pressure** and **financial repression** and **weakened price stability**. Growth stayed around **3 per cent to the 1980s**, about **5 per cent in 1985**.

**Remedies:** **end of automatic monetisation** and a **statutory ceiling on public debt** through the **FRBM Act**, plus greater **co-ordination** between authorities.

**Good practice:** keep **monetary expansion in line with productive capacity**, direct **credit to productive uses**, and **sterilise surplus capital inflows** with **Market Stabilisation Bonds** under the **Market Stabilisation Scheme**.

**Growth vs inflation:** the **2009-11** period saw **high inflation**, with the **repo rate changed more than ten times in two years**; **Subir Gokarn**'s evidence over decades shows **growth rising while inflation fell**, so there is **no long-term trade-off** (stronger still without agriculture).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Automatic monetisation tied the central bank to financing deficits; the FRBM Act and ending ad hocs freed it.

self_check.prompt_text: What was automatic monetisation of the fiscal deficit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The RBI automatically issuing money against renewed ad hoc Treasury Bills to finance the Government.

payload.title: Recent finances of the Centre and States (to 2021-22)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Fiscal stance:** an **infrastructure thrust** (the **National Infrastructure Pipeline** and a **Development Financial Institution** announced in **Union Budget 2021-22**) supports recovery. The Centre chose **gradual consolidation** (a **GFD of 6.8 per cent of GDP for 2021-22**, down from **9.4 per cent**, falling to **below 4.5 per cent by 2025-26**), emphasising **capital expenditure** (**2.5 per cent of GDP** vs an average **1.7 per cent** in 2010-20).

**Support to States (2020-21):** the **WMA limit raised by 60 per cent (April 2020)**, extended by **Advisory Committee on WMA to State Governments (2021)**; **overdraft days** increased; easier **withdrawals from the Consolidated Sinking Fund**; **50-year loans free of interest** for **capital expenditure**; **net market borrowing of up to 4 per cent of GSDP in 2021-22** (more with **power sector reforms**).

**Pandemic package (2020-21):** about **Rs 17.2 lakh crore (9.3 per cent of GDP)**: **PMGKP** (26 March 2020), **Atmanirbhar Bharat 1.0** (liquidity, guarantees for **MSMEs, NBFCs, MFIs, HFCs, DISCOMs**), **2.0** (LTC voucher scheme, capex), **3.0** (housing, **NIIF**, **PLI schemes**). The package **overstates** the fiscal cost because it includes **liquidity measures** (below the line); expenditure rose **Rs 30.4 to 34.5 lakh crore** partly from **bringing food subsidy borrowing on budget** (**FCI loans from NSSF**).

**2021-22:** tax **buoyancy** through **compliance, data analytics, AI** and **faceless assessment**; **disinvestment and asset monetisation** under a new **PSE policy** with **four strategic areas** (atomic energy, space and defence; transport and telecom; power, petroleum, coal and minerals; financial services); heavy **market borrowing** and the **NSSF**.

**States:** GFD-GSDP **3.8 per cent in H1 2020-21 against 2.8 per cent budgeted**; states usually **cut capex by about 0.5 per cent of GDP**; the **17 states** budgeted a **GFD of 3.2 per cent of GSDP in 2021-22** (from **4.1**), through **higher revenue and lower revenue expenditure**; grants slated to rise under **FC-XV**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Counter-cyclical capital spending and state support were the main fiscal responses to the pandemic.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Raised it by 60 per cent over the level on 31 March 2020.

payload.title: Recommendations of the Fifteenth Finance Commission
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Three areas:** **tax devolution**, **grants** and **fiscal roadmap/rules**.

**Tax devolution:** **FC-11** widened the **shareable base to all Union taxes** (excluding **cesses and surcharges**); **FC-14** sharply raised the **devolution ratio** after the **Planning Commission was abolished** and **plan grants ended**. Growth in cesses and surcharges (**outside the divisible pool**) reduced the benefit. **FC-15** kept the **ratio** (adjusted for **Jammu and Kashmir**) for **stability**. **Horizontal sharing** (among States) has used **equity criteria since FC-8**; **FC-15** moved the **population base from 1971 to 2011**, added a **demographic performance** criterion (**to reward population control**: the **inverse of the 2011 total fertility rate times the 1971 population**) and **brought back the tax effort** criterion (used by FC-10 to FC-12, dropped by FC-13 and FC-14).

**Grants:** a **historically high share of grants**; **local body grants** are the **largest**, followed by **revenue deficit grants after devolution**; **grants for particular sectors and States** returned.

**Fiscal rules:** FC-12, 13 and 14 recommended **eliminating revenue deficits** and capping the **fiscal deficit at 3 per cent of GDP**; **FC-12** proposed a **sinking fund** and **guarantee redemption fund** for States; **FC-14** excluded States from **NSSF** operations (from **1 April 2015**). **FC-15** **relaxed targets** after the pandemic: **Union GFD** terminal target **3.5 to 4.5 per cent of GDP by 2025-26**; States' **net borrowing** capped at **4 per cent of GSDP (2021-22)**, **3.5 per cent (2022-23)** and **3 per cent (2023-24 to 2025-26)**, plus **0.5 per cent** incentive borrowing for **power distribution reforms**. The **FRBM Act, 2003** sets targets for **fiscal discipline**.

**Roadmap (dated):** Union GFD from **9.3 to 6.8 per cent of GDP (2021-22 to 2025-26)**, **debt 89.6 per cent peak** and **85.7 per cent by 2025-26**; States' GFD from **6 to 4 per cent of GSDP**, debt **62.9 to 56.6 per cent**; an **inter-departmental group** to review **FRBM**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Devolution, grants and fiscal rules together shape how the Centre and States share and spend resources.

self_check.prompt_text: Which base year for population did FC-15 move to in determining each state share?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 2011, from 1971, with a demographic performance criterion to reward population control.
